text: The Compact cutter comes alongside slowly, like a neighbor, and the lieutenant who hails you sounds as if the day has gone well so far. "Osei, Arcology Compact, patrol. Lovely old freighter. title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The same cutter drifts up on your quarter like a neighbor. "Well, hello again," Osei says. "Last time one of your answers was a little off, and you were so pleasant about it. I remember pleasant." "Now, a small thing, and I'd ask it of anyone." The petty officer is off the band for once, and Osei's voice is the only one. "Sam. Who signed Sam on, and where? The dock, I mean. I'm fond of docks. I grew up above one, and the sound of the lift still gets me in the mornings." Osei laughs, softly, at nothing. "The name of whoever put a pen to it, and the berth number if you have it. That's all. It's not a trap, and I'd tell you if it were. I'm terrible at keeping those."
labels: Answer it, and shade one detail (saying nothing clears less often afterwards)
Answer with "Who's asking?" [60%; if it fails: the stop goes worse, and the captain marks it]

plays.text: You answer, and Osei listens to the whole of it without a sound, which is its own sort of attention. When it's done there's a small warm noise on the band, a sort of hum. "That's lovely," Osei says. "You'd be surprised how many ships get that wrong, in either direction." The petty officer says something off-band, and Osei says, "No, they're fine," in the voice of someone settling a bet. "Right," Osei says. "The crew list, since we're here. I'll go through it nice and slow, like grace before a meal, and we'll all be away in time for tea."

next.title: A Patrol Cutter
next.text: The list reaches Sam Vale, and Osei slows by a single beat, the way a hand slows at a bad rung. "This one is wanted by the Compact," Osei says, and waits. On your deck nobody is looking at Sam, with such care that it amounts to looking. The cutter hasn't moved. Its lock is stowed, and the ticking on the band is its drive keeping pace with yours, which is what a ship does when it means to stay. In the back of the call the petty officer's pen has stopped. You have a few seconds in which the whole next hour belongs to you, and you can feel exactly how few.
labels: [Arcology Compact papers] Vouch for Sam as a member
Pay the officer (400 cr from the ship's fund)
Say nothing and keep Sam below
Hand Sam over to the cutter

nextPlays.text: You send your Arcology Compact papers across on the open band, a scan of the articles with your name and the date, and say Sam is signed on the ship's articles. The cutter's captain takes a long minute with it. You can hear a clerk on the cutter asking if the date is right, and the captain saying it's right. Nothing on your own bridge moves. Then the captain says the articles are in order, notes the stamp, and doesn't ask to see Sam, who is standing eight feet behind you and hasn't breathed in some time. The cutter drops astern, and after a while the feeling comes back into your hands.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You vouched for me to a patrol.

nextPlays.text: You say nothing and keep Sam below, in the engine room, with the hatch dogged. The cutter's captain reads the rest of the crew list and then asks you, evenly, to confirm that everyone on it is aboard. You confirm it. There's a pause long enough that you check whether the band is still open. Then the captain says the list is accepted, and wishes you a clear passage. The cutter holds on your quarter for another three minutes, close enough to read its hull number, before it falls away. Sam comes up from the engine room an hour later with grease on both hands, and doesn't ask anything.

You say nothing and keep Sam below, and the cutter's boarding party finds Sam anyway, in under four minutes, in the crawlway under the galley deck. The fine is 800 cr from the ship's fund, read out over the band. Sam goes across in the cutter's launch between two of the patrol's people, not in restraints, but not free to stop either. At the lock Sam looks back once, and not at you. Your crew crowds the viewport and watches the launch the whole way. Nobody tells you what they think, and nobody needs to. Sofia signs on for the berth.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: A wanted crew member was found aboard.
9 Jul 2214: You kept me aboard and I was found.

nextPlays.text: Sam goes across in the cutter's launch without a word, because Sam understands that there's nothing to say that would do any good now. The launch is small and grey and has a number on it. Sam sits in the stern with both hands on the thwart and looks at the deck, not at you. When the launch is clear the cutter's captain comes on the band and thanks you for your cooperation, and says it will be noted. You don't ask where. The cutter breaks off and falls astern. Nobody on your deck moves for a long moment, and the one who moves first is the one who goes to check that the airlock is still sealed. Daniel signs on for the berth.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You handed me to a patrol of the Compact.

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The same cutter drifts up on your quarter like a neighbor. "Well, hello again," Osei says. "Last time you asked who was asking, and I went and told the whole mess. They still laugh." "Now, a small thing, and I'd ask it of anyone." The petty officer is off the band for once, and Osei's voice is the only one. "Sam. Who signed Sam on, and where? The dock, I mean. I'm fond of docks. I grew up above one, and the sound of the lift still gets me in the mornings." Osei laughs, softly, at nothing. "The name of whoever put a pen to it, and the berth number if you have it. That's all. It's not a trap, and I'd tell you if it were. I'm terrible at keeping those."

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The same cutter drifts up on your quarter like a neighbor. "Well, hello again," Osei says. "Last time you asked who was asking. I wasn't offended. I'm told I should have been." "Now, a small thing, and I'd ask it of anyone." The petty officer is off the band for once, and Osei's voice is the only one. "Sam. Who signed Sam on, and where? The dock, I mean. I'm fond of docks. I grew up above one, and the sound of the lift still gets me in the mornings." Osei laughs, softly, at nothing. "The name of whoever put a pen to it, and the berth number if you have it. That's all. It's not a trap, and I'd tell you if it were. I'm terrible at keeping those."

title: A Patrol Cutter
text: The Concord frigate holds a hundred kilometers off and speaks first, which is correct procedure, and the officer who speaks is correct about everything else too. "Commander Varga, Dome Concord, aboard the frigate," the voice says. "Thank you for matching. The crew list will wait one moment, and I would be obliged for a complete answer." A pen scratches somewhere behind the voice. "Who signed Sam onto your articles, and at which dock? The name, please, and the dock." Varga waits, and you can hear the pen waiting too. "I write what's said to me," Varga says, "exactly as it's said. Please bear that in mind."

plays.text: You answer, and Varga reads it back to you, word for word, slowly enough that you can hear how it sounds in someone else's voice. It sounds fine. "Thank you," Varga says. text: Varga is on the band again, at the same distance, with the same pen. "Dome Concord remembers you," Varga says. "Last time one of your answers did not hold. I have it written. text: Varga is on the band again, at the same distance, with the same pen. "Dome Concord remembers you," Varga says. "Last time you asked who was asking. I gave my name twice, and you said you hadn't caught it. It's written down, in both places." The pen is already moving. "Your articles, please, and the date of your last landing. The date, and the dock." Somewhere behind Varga a second voice reads a number from a screen, and Varga says, "Thank you, not yet." The frigate hasn't moved closer, and doesn't need to. "I will read your answer back to you," Varga says, "so that we both hear it. If a word is wrong, now is the moment to say so. It is a courtesy, and it is only offered the once."

text: It's Teague again, on the same band, with the same collar and a new slate. "We've met," Teague says. "You had it right last time, so I'll ask something else." title: A Patrol Cutter
text: It's Teague again, on the same band, with the same collar and a new slate. "We've met," Teague says. "Last time you asked who was asking. I said it twice. I won't say it a third time, so I'll just ask something else." The petty officer in the background leans over a screen. "Cargo seals. Read me the numbers off your hold, bow to stern, and don't go and look them up." You can hear the cutter ticking as it matches your thrust. "Last ship that read me seals off a manifest had two of them reversed," Teague says. "The crew list is next, either way. I'd just like to know what kind of ship I'm reading it to." The pen is out. It's the same pen.

text: Sam has been at the news feed in the galley since the war began between the Compact and the Concord. At Earth Sam finds you. "My people are in it," Sam says. "I'd like to go home and see if I can help. I'll understand if you say no."

plays.text: Captain Vance is at the galley table with the notebook, and doesn't close it when you sit down. "Forty-two hundred," the captain says. "My first bad call, on an ore hauler, when I was the senior hand. Shielding lashed for a two-g burn, and we ran at three, and I watched the straps go and logged it after the paperwork was in." A line goes into the book. "Forty-two hundred for the cargo. The late log cost me the berth." Two more lines go in. "This run we're lashed for two-g, and we burn at one point eight." (+2 experience at the gunner post.)

plays.text: Ines loads a bad approach into the sim and gives you the left seat: a crosswind at the pad, a stale vector from the tower, one thruster late. You fly it into the deck. "You flared," she says, before the board has finished going red. "Stop first. Then flare." She resets it. On the second run she hums with her eyes shut and corrects you twice without opening them, once aloud and once by tapping the throttle with one finger. The third goes into the deck as well, and she resets it without a word. The sixth comes down inside the numbers, and she writes the time in her logbook. "Tomorrow, same hour," she says, already unstrapping. "I'll make the tower lie both ways." (+3 experience at the pilot post.)
mem: 9 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Tomas takes you down the coolant loop on a slow watch, valve by valve, with the engine room door propped open. She likes the air, he says. To the pipes he talks low, in Igbo, and doesn't stop. To you he gives each valve's name and what it's for, and nothing else, until the fourth, where he takes your hand and puts it flat on the line beside his. "Feel that? Pump. The bearing's behind it." He takes the hand back. "When you can feel the bearing, come and get me." He holds out the spanner handle-first. "Quarter turn. Properly." You turn it a quarter. The pipe over your head ticks twice and settles, and he starts telling it something in Igbo, and he's still telling it when the watch bell goes. (+3 experience at the engineer post.)
mem: 9 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Yelena runs the range sim with the ring-ball feed up on the second screen, the Olympus Ravens two down at the half, and she coaches both. "Not there. Where the next pass goes," she says to you, and to the Ravens' keeper, at the same volume, "Where are you going? Where is he going? Look at him!" She calls her own shots before they land, gets four of five, and swears at the fifth until the sim resets. When the Ravens score she stands up, and sits down again rubbing the knee. You hit three of your last five. "Better," she says, without looking around. They lose by one. She turns the feed off. "Referee's from Hellas," she says, and runs your set again from the top. (+3 experience at the gunner post.)

plays.text: Ruben hands you a thermos and half a stack of intercepts, and the two of you sort them at the console into three piles, which he labels TRUE, FALSE and LOVELY on strips of tape. He talks the whole time. "This one says Hellas is short of filters. Hellas is short of filters every time they lose a tech, and they lost two in June." He holds it up to the light. "I wrote this. Eleven years ago. They've kept my wording." It goes on LOVELY. The relay on Valles was down for six days once, and he tells you what that did to the water schedule, and about a woman who sent him a recipe through a firewall. "It was good. I made it twice." He shows you the tells: a timestamp in the wrong decade, a callsign that's too polite. By the end of the watch LOVELY is the tallest pile. Ruben squares it with both hands and starts on the second half of the stack. (+3 experience at the comms post.)
mem: 9 Jul 2214: We spent some downtime together.

plays.text: Bexa takes you down to the hold to rig the tether winch on a crate, the way she'd rig it on a hatch. She shows you the hitch the Ceres tugs use, which the manual calls wrong. "Manual's never towed anything." While you tie it, she tells you about a tug crew at Ceres who tried to bring in a freighter with a cargo net, and what the harbor master said on the open band, which she gives you exactly, twice: "Tug four, that is not a line, that is a hope." Your third hitch holds under the winch's full pull. Your fourth jams the drum. Bexa looks at it, then at the clock. "Leave it," she says. "Next watch. It'll still be jammed." (+3 experience at the pilot post.)

plays.text: You cook something real out of the good stores: garlic, rice in the pressure pot, and the block of butter that has been missing a corner for a week. "Who had the butter?" "Nobody had the butter." "The butter has teeth marks." Everyone off watch comes to the galley, which seats five, and the rest eat standing with bowls passed over shoulders. The engineer eats in the doorway with one foot in the corridor, in case. Seconds run out before the last two get any, and the crust in the pot goes to whoever has the next watch.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: The captain shared a meal with us.

plays.text: You call it, and the klaxon goes, and the whole ship comes off its bunks at once. Damage control first: the closers on the section doors, the patch kits from the locker by the lock, a hose run out along a corridor eleven feet wide. Then the guns, against the stopwatch, with the loaders swearing at the loaders. Then damage control again, because the watch said so, and one argument about whose fault the fire in the galley was, which was a drill fire and nobody's. Four minutes ten, start to finish; the number on the card by the hatch is three-forty. Nobody enjoys it. When it's done the crew sit on the deck with their backs to the frame, breathing, and someone says, "Again at the flip," and gets no answer. (Better odds in a fight for the rest of this burn.)

You spend a watch crawling the frame with a heat gun, a tin of compound and a flashlight in your teeth, filling old scars one plate at a time: a seam by the aft lock that has wept since Ceres, a dent in the cargo bay wall that nobody has owned up to, a hand's width of bead gone brittle along a patch. The compound takes forty minutes to set and smells of hot pennies. Hull 40 to 50 of 50. It's slow work, all of it yours, with no one to say whether the last seam is good. You sit against the wall with your hands black to the wrist until the compound stops smelling.

You make the rounds of the berths, knocking on each door in turn and waiting for the closer to cycle. You hear out a complaint about the air recycler, a story about a cousin on Ganymede who won a boat at cards and lost it by the following week, and a request for an extra blanket, which you've got. From one passenger, the quiet one in the end berth, you get a question: whether it's normal to feel this far from everything. You promise to look into the recycler. You tell them it is.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: The captain came to check on us.

plays.text: You run the flip drill on the sim: cut the drive, swing the ship end over end, and light it again on the new heading, smoothly enough that nothing loose aboard moves. That is what the sim scores. The first flip puts a tool roll and two bulbs of coffee into the air on the sim's deck plan. After that most of the ship stays put, and the sim flags the restart as two seconds late every time. (+3 experience at the pilot post.)

You spend a watch on the range sim, tracking and leading targets: two hundred rounds, the first sixty of them spent on where the target was. The sim gives you a score and a lane-by-lane breakdown. Your worst lane is the curved one, which is the one a real raider takes. (+3 experience at the gunner post.)

You go through the plant one system at a time, with the manual open on your knee and a meter in your teeth, and find two things nobody wrote down: a gauge that reads four percent high, and a bracket held on by habit. You pencil them inside the cover of the manual, under the last note in the margin, which is dated eleven years ago. (+3 experience at the engineer post.)

You sit on the bands for a watch, learning the rhythm of a dozen stations: who comes up on the hour, who stays on after the tower has told them to clear, who reads the weather slowly enough to be copied by hand. You learn which of them lie about their transponders by the way a callsign drifts a digit when the traffic is thin. You log four, and a fifth at the end of the watch. (+3 experience at the comms post.)
There's nothing to practice.

plays.text: She talks you through it like a commentator: the flare a second too late, the crosswind he hasn't read, the thrust he'll wish he had saved. He clips the gantry, gently, as she said he would, and she raises her glass to the screen. "Eleven out of ten for effort," she says.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You watched a bad landing with me, and I enjoyed the company.

plays.text: She turns from the screen. "The ferry ran every forty minutes," she says. "Nine years. I knew the regulars by their shoes. There was an old man who rode the 6:40 every morning to feed the pigeons on the Luna side. I never spoke to him once. I'd give a great deal to know if he still does." She drinks. "I only ever saw the back of his head."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You asked about Lisbon, and I told you.

title: Third Approach
text: In the dock bar, Ines Ferreira has the stool nearest the docking screen. A pilot on it's making a poor job of an approach. "Third attempt," she says, without turning. "He's going to clip the gantry." She keeps her eyes on the screen. "When somebody lands badly, I used to buy the controller a drink. It's not the controller's fault. Nobody remembers that."

plays.text: You go together, and it takes her three tries to say her name. The controller hears all of it: the pad, the order, the forty-one. "I was on the desk that night," the controller says. "It wasn't my call. Everyone on the desk knew who'd put that shuttle down. It was the best landing I've seen." Ines says nothing. She shakes the controller's hand, and keeps hold of it.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You went over to the controller with me.

plays.text: You say nothing, and she doesn't go over. She finishes her drink and puts the glass down with a click. "Not tonight," she says. On the way out she looks back once at the badge, and then straight ahead.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You let me decide about the controller.

title: The Badge
text: Someone at the end of the bar is wearing a tower controller's badge, and Ines has stopped moving. The crest is Lisbon's. "It could be nothing," she says to her glass. "There are four hundred of them. It's almost certainly not the one who gave the order." She hasn't looked round. Her hand is flat on the bar, and the knuckles are white.

plays.text: A round for the dock crew turns into three hours. Tomas is shown the jig they use for the rail, and a trick for a seam that has given him trouble since the ring, and he shows them one of his own. He walks back to the ship with a notebook full of sketches. "They talk to the work," he says. "The same as me."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You bought a round for the dock crew, and let me talk shop.

plays.text: You take a stool at the other end of the bar and leave them to it. Every so often a burst of technical argument comes down the bar, with hand gestures. When Tomas finds you, hours later, he's hoarse, and holds up a hand with a new burn across the knuckle. "Thank you," he says. "He let me try the jig."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You let me talk shop with a welder.

title: Shop Talk
text: Tomas Achebe has found a welder at the bar: a working one, in dock coveralls, with burn scars on both wrists and a nervous laugh. They've been talking for an hour. "Look at the bead," Tomas says to you, low, with a hand on the bar rail. "Look at that. Somebody welded this properly. Nobody does that for a bar."

Let him have his shop talk

plays.text: The delay is eleven seconds. You say your name and wait. A small voice says, in a rush: "He never says he has people. I'm glad. Are you feeding him?" Tomas looks at the floor. "Eleven seconds," he says afterwards, "and she heard every word."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You said hello to my sister.

plays.text: You wave. He grins, holds the handset up to the glass, and says something to her in Igbo. When he comes out of the booth he doesn't talk for the rest of the evening, and you leave him to it.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You waved to my sister from across the room.

title: A Call to Lagos Ring
text: The bar has a row of call booths at the back. In the last one, with the door open a hand's width, Tomas Achebe is on a long-distance link to his sister. You can hear his half, loud the way people are across a delay: "No, it was paid. Yes. I promise. Eat something." He sees you, covers the handset, and beckons. "Would you say hello? She doesn't believe I have a crew."

plays.text: She explains it to him with a fork, a beer mat and a great many examples, and you stand behind her with your arms folded. It doesn't come to blows. It comes to him buying a round and apologizing to the memory of number seven. At the end he asks for her autograph. She signs the beer mat. "Ravens," she says to the room.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You backed me up when a stranger insulted the Ravens.

plays.text: "He's wrong," she says, all the way to the door and halfway down the dock. "He's so wrong." She lets you take her arm. Halfway to the ship she stops, and laughs, and says it was probably for the best, because she'd have hit him. "Thank you," she says. "I needed somebody to be the sensible one."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You steered me out before it turned into a thing.

title: Last Orders, Ravens
text: The bar is showing a ring-ball replay, and a loud man at the next table has said something about the Olympus Dome Ravens. Yelena Quint puts her drink down. "He's wrong," she says to you, evenly. "He's wrong about the offside rule, and he's wrong about number seven, and he's wrong about my knee." She's already standing. "I'm going to explain this to him."

plays.text: You say you'll take it. The girl goes red, and Yelena crouches down and puts an arm around her. She asks the girl her name and her position. It's goalkeeper. "Good," Yelena says. "Nobody ever thanks the goalkeeper." When the picture is taken she signs the shirt in full, and says nothing about the knee.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You took a picture of me with a girl in my old shirt.

plays.text: You look at the bar. When you look back, Yelena is in a booth with the girl, the shirt on the table between them, showing her something with a salt cellar and two beer mats. It goes on for forty minutes. When the girl leaves she's almost running. Yelena says nothing about it. She's humming the Ravens' song.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You gave me room with the girl in the old shirt.

title: Number Seven

plays.text: A round loosens the bartender in about a minute, and Ruben is leaning forward with a pencil before the glasses are down. By the end of the night you have the news of three docks, and one item worth money: A trade fair on Juno Commons has brought in a great many merchants, and Luxury Goods is going for a song. Ruben puts the pencil behind his ear. "A good listener has no name," he says. "A good bartender has a hundred."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You bought a round, and the bartender talked.

plays.text: You sit with them and say little. The bartender talks about the dock office, a wedding, a shortage. Ruben listens without a word. When you leave, he says, "You have the gift. People tell you things."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You listened with me.

title: The Bartender Who Listens
text: Ruben Castellanos has made a friend of the bartender, or the bartender of him. They've been trading news since the doors opened: who's short of what, which dock office is slow, whose cousin is getting married. "Nobody tells a bartender anything," Ruben says to you. "They tell him everything. He's the best comms officer on the station and he doesn't know it."

plays.text: You walk over and say you work with a man who knows more about the dome network than anyone alive. The councillor goes still. "Castellanos," she says. "The relay in the kitchen." She looks past you at the menu. "We lost eleven days of band because of what he did, and afterward we found out he had saved the north dome. I've been trying to find him for four years." Ruben lowers the menu all the way.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You introduced yourself to the councillor who signed my notice.

plays.text: You don't move. Ruben stays behind the menu, and the councillor takes a table at the far end, orders, and doesn't look round. After twenty minutes she leaves. Ruben puts the menu down. "Thank you," he says. "I couldn't have said it. Another day." He picks up the thermos and offers it to you.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You let me hide behind the menu.

title: The Council Member
text: A gray-haired woman in a good coat has come into the bar with two aides, and Ruben Castellanos has picked up the menu and is holding it high. "That's Councillor Reyes," he says, from behind it. "Of the Valles dome council. She signed my notice." He lowers it an inch. "I've practiced what I'd say to her for four years. I can't remember any of it."

plays.text: She tells you, and it takes a while, and every name is in it: the engineer who sang, the child with the broken wrist, the captain, who wouldn't leave the bridge until everyone else was off. "She's for sale again," she says, looking at the card. "They never fixed the port thruster. I told them about the port thruster." She says nothing else for a time.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You asked about the crew of the Honest Comet.

plays.text: You put a drink at her elbow and say nothing. She reads the board from one end to the other, card by card, saying a ship's name now and then under her breath. When she has finished she lifts the glass. "Thank you," she says. "It's good to be somewhere I can be quiet. It's better with someone who knows how."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You bought me a drink and let me read the board.

title: Hull Numbers
text: The bar has a salvage chit board by the door, where claims are pinned for anyone who wants to buy a hull number and a chance. Bexa Oyelaran has been standing in front of it for ten minutes, reading, her lips moving. "I know this one," she says, and touches a card. "The Honest Comet. I towed her into Ceres eleven years ago. She was dark for six weeks. Everyone aboard was alive." She keeps her finger on the card.
labels: Buy her a drink and let her read

plays.text: You take a stool at the other end and watch, without listening. They talk for an hour. She listens, mostly, with her hand around her glass, and he talks with his hands, drawing the tug in the air. At the end she takes a pen on a chain from her jacket and signs the back of the postcard, small and even. She puts it in her jacket, where the list is.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You left me to talk to the boy from Pallas.

plays.text: You sit down beside her. Her shoulder comes to rest against yours. The boy tells it all: the dark, the cold, the drawing. He says she was the first person he ever saw who wasn't afraid. Bexa says, in a low voice, "I was terrified." The boy laughs, startled. She smiles. It's the first time you've seen all of her face.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You sat with me while the boy from Pallas talked.

title: The Boy from Pallas
text: A young man of about twenty has stopped in front of Bexa at the bar, holding a postcard. It has a crayon drawing on it: a small tug and a big dark ship. "You pulled my ship in," he says. "Eleven years ago. I was nine. I've drawn it every year since." Bexa puts down her glass. She's looking at the postcard, and not at him.

plays.text: You say, "Take it," and Pax does, with the stranger a hand's width away and a crowd gathering. The first dart goes dead center. The second goes into the first. The stranger whistles low. Pax's hands haven't shaken, and Pax looks at them. "That," Pax says to you on the walk back, "wasn't as bad as I thought."
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You told me to take the shot, and I did.

plays.text: You step up and play badly and lose and pay. Pax watches from a stool, grinning. At the end Pax says, solemnly, "Your stance is wrong," and corrects it, standing very close, without a flinch. The stranger gives a slow nod. Pax doesn't see it. You do.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You played the stranger so that I didn't have to.

title: The Dart Board
text: The dart-laser board is free, and a stranger in a ring-hand's jacket has seen Pax Iwu looking at it. "Fancy a game?" they say over the noise. "Loser pays." Pax has gone quiet. "The hands are fine," Pax says. "The hands are always fine. It's the people beside them." Then, to you, barely audible: "I'd be good at it if they wouldn't stand so close."

plays.text: It's eleven lines, plain and exact: that Pax is sorry, that Pax isn't sure what for, that Pax is learning to stand beside the thing. "It's good," you say. Pax reads it once more, breathes in, and sends it fast, before changing their mind. Then Pax sits down on the nearest stool with the handheld on their knee, and shakes.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You read my letter to the foreman, and said it was good.

plays.text: "I think so," Pax says. Pax reads it over twice. "Yes. I think so. I'm not good at saying it, and I'd rather say it badly than not at all." Pax sends it. Afterward you have a glass of water together, and neither of you says much.
mem: 25 Dec 2214: You asked me if I really wanted to send it.

title: A Letter Answered
text: The bar has a message terminal at the back, a battered one, with a curtain. Pax Iwu has been in front of it for the better part of an hour, typing and deleting. At last Pax comes to find you, holding the handheld at arm's length. "I've written back to the foreman," Pax says. "It's eleven lines. I don't know if it's right. Will you read it?"
labels: Read it and say it's good
Ask if they really want to send it

plays.text: She goes in, and the scram goes home, and the alarm winds down through its notes into silence. She comes out with her sleeves burnt through and her hands steady, and sits on the deck for a minute. "Routine," she says, and writes it in the log. Captain Adair has come down the passage without any of his speeches, and stands at the door.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me go into the reactor, and I came out.

plays.text: She goes in first, and the housing is hotter than the board said, and for three minutes the only sound on the bridge is the alarm. She comes out held up between two crew, and the hand that found the scram doesn't close properly, and won't. She sits down on the deck by the door. "It's off," she says. "Tell him the plant is off. He'll want to know it's all right."
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me go into the reactor, and I came out.

plays.text: She goes in first, as she said she would, and the door closes behind her. The reactor board drops to nothing, and then, for a moment, to everything. You wait at the door for a long time after it's quiet. Captain Adair is the first one there. He doesn't speak. He puts his hand on the shielded door.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: We lost Ilsa at the reactor.

plays.text: He goes to the lock with the sheet in his hand, and talks for eleven minutes, in a level voice, about the odds. The long ship backs off. He comes back with his coat buttoned wrong and says, "They've agreed to wait," and sits down on the lock coaming and doesn't say anything else for a while. Captain Pell doesn't make a joke. She puts a hand on his shoulder, and takes it off again.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me go to the lock, and I came back.

plays.text: He goes to the lock with the sheet, and it goes wrong at the second sentence, and for a minute the only sound is shouting through a hatch. He comes back carried, with a cut over one eye, and the hand that held the sheet is closed round it and won't open properly. "They've agreed to wait," he says. "I told them the odds."
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me go to the lock, and I came back.

plays.text: He goes to the lock alone, with the sheet in his hand, and the lock cycles, and what the people on the other side do isn't something the board can tell you. When the lock opens again, he's not what's in it. Captain Pell comes down from the guns slowly, with the grin gone, and stands at the lock without moving. "He told me," she says. "Every time. He told me."
mem: 9 Jul 2214: We lost Ansel at the lock.

plays.text: She brings her in by hand, and the ship settles into the berth like a coin into a slot. Pilar lets go of the stick and flexes her fingers. "Four minutes," she says. "Enter that." Captain Sato enters it, word for word, and under it, in their own hand, writes: Correct.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me fly the approach by hand, and I came out.

plays.text: She brings her in by hand, and the crosswind catches the ship at the last four meters, and the stick kicks. She lands her by main strength and nothing else, and the hand that held the stick doesn't close properly, and won't. "It's in the berth," she says. "Enter that."
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me fly the approach by hand, and I came out.

plays.text: She brings her in by hand. The crosswind takes the ship at the last moment, and for a long second the bridge is the sound of the stick in her hands. The gate crew say afterwards it was the cleanest approach they had seen, until the last four meters. Captain Sato enters it in the log, in the same hand as every other entry, and then sits for a long time with the pen over the next line.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: We lost Pilar at the helm.

plays.text: He goes in, and the pod is lashed, and the load stops. He comes out with ice in his beard and a cut across one knuckle, and sits down on the hatch coaming to get his breath. "That's where it goes," he says. Captain Vance looks at the hold, and at him, and says nothing, and writes it down.
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me go into the hold, and I came out.

plays.text: He goes in first, and it goes wrong at the number two strap, and the hold is nothing but ice and shouting. He comes out carried, and the hand that held the strap doesn't close properly, and won't. The med kit is already open. He says, from the deck, "Number two is lashed. So that's done."
mem: 9 Jul 2214: You let me go into the hold, and I came out.

plays.text: He goes in first, as he said he would. The strap holds, and the pod doesn't, and the board shows nothing you can read. You get the hatch open from your side. By then the hold is quiet. title: At the Reactor
text: The reactor alarm is a rising note that you feel in the deck before you hear it. The coolant loop has lost pressure, and the board shows the pile heating faster than the pumps can carry it. Ilsa is already at the shielded door, pulling on gloves. "There's a manual scram at the back of the housing," she says. "I know where it is. Nobody else does. Give me three minutes." She says it to the bridge, item by item. The plant is in good order. Kwame has the med kit open at the door. The engineer is suiting up behind her. She waits for your answer, and has already started on the second glove.

plays.text: You give the word, and the guns speak, and the long ship answers, and for a minute it's loud and bright and Pell is laughing. The hull takes what it takes. title: The Fight She Shouldn't Have Picked
text: A ship has come up on your stern, long and dark, and it's one of Dobrescu's. Captain Pell has seen it on the board and is already at the guns, laughing, with a figure in her head. "We can take her," she says. "We could take her." Ansel is at the boarding lock with his coat on and the sheet in one hand. "I'd like to speak to them," he says. "Give me ten minutes, and the lock, and don't fire." He says it flat. Your hull is sound. Kwame has the med kit open at the lock. Nobody else is on the guns. plays.text: You tell her no, and call the go-round. The ship stands off from the gate, and the ice sits in the hold, and the cells burn for the second pass. Pilar takes her hands off the stick one at a time. "It's your call," she says. "It was always going to be somebody's."

title: The Docking Emergency
text: The gate's tractor beam fails twenty seconds out, and the ship is carrying forty tonnes of ice at a closing speed the berth was never meant for. The nav display is lagging. title: Signing On
text:
The queue at the foot of the elevator is kept by the berth book, and a clerk won't stamp a book until the shifts owed on it are stood. Yours has two seasons of gate duty in it and no berth. The berths go to people with a cousin, and you have a trade and no cousin. The card was pinned to the notice board at the arcology docks, in pencil: HAND WANTED, ICE HAULER, DEPARTS WHEN FULL. The Iron Anvil, an ice hauler out of Earth, took you for what you could do. Captain Hester Vance reads your papers twice. The second time she has a pencil, and she writes your wage into a ruled notebook before she looks up. "35 a day and 6 percent of what we clear," she says. "That's the whole of it. I won't surprise you, and I'd like you not to surprise me."

You have the helm: Captain Hester Vance plots the run, and you fly it, by hand.

Captain Hester Vance picks each run and carries freight for a shipper, who pays on delivery. Errands for wherever she's going come through the port, and the captain keeps a fifth. Why did you sign on?

The queue at the foot of the elevator is kept by the berth book, and a clerk won't stamp a book until the shifts owed on it are stood. Yours has two seasons of gate duty in it and no berth. The berths go to people with a cousin, and you have a trade and no cousin. The card was pinned to the notice board at the arcology docks, in pencil: HAND WANTED, ICE HAULER, DEPARTS WHEN FULL. The Iron Anvil, an ice hauler out of Earth, took you for what you could do. Captain Hester Vance reads your papers twice. The second time she has a pencil, and she writes your wage into a ruled notebook before she looks up. "35 a day and 6 percent of what we clear," she says. "That's the whole of it. I won't surprise you, and I'd like you not to surprise me."

You have the plant: the reactor's output, the heat and the wear are yours to watch, and yours to break.

Captain Hester Vance picks each run and carries freight for a shipper, who pays on delivery. Errands for wherever she's going come through the port, and the captain keeps a fifth. Why did you sign on?

plays.text: You work it out on the ramp, on your fingers: 35 a day, and 8 percent of every run now, 2 points up on what you were offered, and no cousin needed. The berth book goes in the bottom of the bag.
At the first bulkhead you stop and ask what the placard says, and someone tells you. By the end of the hour you've asked eleven more questions. The twelfth is to the cook, and the answer is a tray.
You stow your bag behind the third door on the left and don't go back down the ramp. The hatch shuts on its closer. Down on the water the tide gates sound at the turn. Then they don't.

next.title: The Room in Hermes Foundry
next.text: It has been 20 days. The latch sticks worse in the damp, and Duarte has put a rag in the gap under the door against it. There is dust on the sill and none on the bed. "We kept it aired," Duarte says, and it comes out sounding like an apology. There is a letter on the table with your name on it in Duarte's hand. It was left here, and not sent to the dock. The bag of galley tea you left is on the hook behind the door, and it is lighter. You have slept in it once before.
labels: Look in, and go back to the ship
